en.title: What an economy is; GDP
objectives: Explain what an economy does and who takes part in it
Describe what GDP measures and what it leaves out
Compare GDP and GDP per person across countries
en.hook: Sri Lanka's economy shrank sharply in 2022, then returned to growth. What exactly shrank, and how do economists measure it?

sections.body: An economy is the system that decides what is produced, how and for whom. Households sell their work and buy goods; firms hire workers and sell products; the government taxes, spends and sets rules. Every purchase is someone else's income, which is why spending, income and output are three views of the same activity.

Gross domestic product (GDP) is the market value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a period, usually a quarter or a year. It can be counted three ways: total spending (consumption, investment, government and net exports), total income, or total output by sector. Real GDP removes the effect of price changes, so it shows whether more was actually produced.

GDP leaves out unpaid work at home, much informal activity and damage to the environment. It also says nothing about how income is shared. That is why economists also look at GDP per person, poverty rates and broader measures such as the Human Development Index.

example.title: Reading a growth figure (illustrative)
steps: Real GDP last year: Rs 100 trillion.
Real GDP this year: Rs 104 trillion.
If the population grew 1%, GDP per person grew about 3%.

lens.local: Sri Lanka's Department of Census and Statistics publishes GDP every quarter. Services make up the largest share of output, followed by industry and agriculture.
lens.regional: India and Bangladesh have been among the fastest-growing large economies in Asia, while China's growth has slowed from double digits in the 2000s to around 5%.
lens.global: The United States has the largest economy at market exchange rates and China the second. Comparisons often use purchasing power parity (PPP), which adjusts for price differences between countries.

en.takeaway: GDP measures how much a country produces, not how well its people live; read it alongside GDP per person and how income is shared.
sources: Department of Census and Statistics, Sri Lanka: national accounts
IMF World Economic Outlook database
World Bank World Development Indicators

en.title: What inflation is; price indices worldwide
objectives: Define inflation and deflation
Explain how a consumer price index is built
Compare how countries measure and target inflation
en.hook: In 2022, prices in Sri Lanka rose faster than at any time in decades, with inflation peaking near 70% a year. Bread, bus fares and gas cylinders all cost far more within months.

sections.body: Inflation is a general rise in prices over time, so each rupee buys less. It is usually quoted as the percentage change in a price index over the past 12 months. Deflation is the opposite, a general fall in prices, which sounds good but often comes with falling wages and weak demand.

sections.h: How a price index is built
sections.body: Statisticians choose a basket of goods and services that a typical household buys: food, rent, transport, health, education and more. Each item gets a weight based on how much households spend on it. Prices are collected every month and combined into one number; inflation is the change in that number.
Headline inflation includes everything in the basket. Core inflation leaves out volatile items such as fresh food and energy, which makes the underlying trend easier to see. Central banks watch both.

example.title: Calculating inflation from an index (illustrative)
steps: A basket that cost Rs 1,000 a year ago now costs about Rs 1,050.

lens.local: Sri Lanka publishes two indices: the Colombo Consumer Price Index (CCPI) for the Colombo district and the National Consumer Price Index (NCPI) for the whole country. The Central Bank uses CCPI for its inflation target.
lens.regional: India's main measure is the all-India Consumer Price Index; the Reserve Bank of India targets 4% within a band of 2% to 6%. Japan spent much of the 1990s to the 2010s struggling with deflation.
lens.global: In the United States the CPI is widely reported, but the Federal Reserve targets 2% inflation measured by the PCE price index. The euro area uses the harmonised index, HICP.

en.takeaway: Inflation is the rate at which money loses buying power; always ask which index is being quoted.
sources: Department of Census and Statistics, Sri Lanka: CCPI and NCPI
Central Bank of Sri Lanka: monetary policy reports
Reserve Bank of India: monetary policy framework
US Bureau of Labor Statistics: CPI

en.title: What money is; what central banks do
objectives: Describe the three jobs money does
Explain how bank lending creates money
List the main tasks of a central bank
en.hook: A Rs 5,000 note costs only a few rupees to print, yet shops accept it for goods worth Rs 5,000. Why?

sections.body: Money has three jobs. It is a medium of exchange, so people do not need to barter. It is a unit of account, so prices can be compared. And it is a store of value, so income earned today can be spent later. Money works because people trust it will be accepted tomorrow.

Notes and coins are issued by the central bank, but most money is bank deposits. When a bank makes a loan it credits the borrower's account, creating a new deposit. The central bank influences how much lending happens through interest rates and rules.

A central bank keeps prices stable, issues currency, supervises banks, manages the country's foreign reserves and acts as lender of last resort in a crisis. Most modern central banks are given a clear target, usually low and stable inflation, and some independence to pursue it.

example.title: How a loan creates money
steps: You deposit Rs 100,000 in cash at Bank A.
Bank A lends Rs 80,000 to a shop owner by crediting her account.
Deposits now total Rs 180,000, though only Rs 100,000 of cash came in.
When the loan is repaid, that Rs 80,000 of deposit money disappears.

lens.local: The Central Bank of Sri Lanka was set up in 1950. The Central Bank of Sri Lanka Act of 2023 made domestic price stability its main objective and strengthened its independence.
lens.regional: The Reserve Bank of India (founded in 1935), the People's Bank of China and the Bank of Japan manage three of the world's largest economies. Their decisions move currencies across Asia.
lens.global: The US Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and the Bank of England are the most closely watched central banks. Because so much world trade is priced in dollars, Fed decisions affect almost every country.

en.takeaway: Money works because of trust, and central banks exist to protect that trust by keeping prices and banks stable.
sources: Central Bank of Sri Lanka Act, No. 16 of 2023
Bank of England: Money creation in the modern economy (2014)
Reserve Bank of India: history

en.title: Taxes and national budgets
objectives: Explain where government revenue comes from
Describe deficits, surpluses and the primary balance
Compare tax levels across countries
en.hook: Every year the Finance Minister presents a budget that changes what you pay in VAT, income tax and fees. Where does the money go, and what happens when it is not enough?

sections.body: Governments raise money through taxes on income, on spending (VAT, excise and customs duties) and on property and profits. Some revenue also comes from fees, state enterprises and grants. Taxes on spending are easier to collect but take a bigger share of poorer households' income.

sections.h: What the money is spent on
sections.body: Spending pays for public services such as health, education, defence and roads; salaries and pensions of public servants; welfare transfers; and interest on past borrowing. Spending on long-lived assets such as roads and power plants is called capital spending.

sections.h: Deficits, surpluses and the primary balance
sections.body: When spending is greater than revenue, the government runs a deficit and must borrow. The primary balance is the balance before interest payments; it shows whether today's policies are adding to debt. A surplus means revenue exceeds spending.

example.title: Reading a simple budget (illustrative)
steps: Primary balance = 4.0 − 3.8 = Rs 0.2 trillion surplus; overall balance = 4.0 − 3.8 − 2.5 = Rs 2.3 trillion deficit.

lens.local: Sri Lanka has had one of the lowest ratios of tax revenue to GDP in the world, and interest payments take a large share of revenue. Raising revenue has been a central goal of recent budgets and of the IMF-supported programme.
lens.regional: India collects taxes at national and state level and introduced a nationwide Goods and Services Tax (GST) in 2017. Many South and Southeast Asian countries collect between 10% and 20% of GDP in tax.
lens.global: France and Denmark collect over 40% of GDP in taxes and social contributions, while the United States collects about a quarter. Higher taxes usually pay for broader public services and pensions.

en.takeaway: A budget is a plan for who pays and who benefits; the primary balance shows whether debt is being brought under control.
sources: Ministry of Finance, Sri Lanka: annual budget documents
IMF: Sri Lanka programme reviews
OECD Revenue Statistics

en.title: Imports, exports, tourism and remittances
objectives: Explain why countries trade
Identify the main sources of foreign currency for Sri Lanka
Read a simple trade balance
en.hook: Sri Lanka imports almost all its fuel and most of its medicines. To pay for them it needs dollars. Where do those dollars come from?

sections.body: Countries trade because each can produce some things relatively cheaply. Sri Lanka grows tea and makes clothing efficiently, while importing fuel and machinery costs less than producing them. Trade lets everyone consume more than they could alone.

Exports of goods (tea, apparel, rubber products) and services (tourism, IT, shipping) earn foreign currency; imports use it. Money sent home by citizens working abroad, called remittances, is another major inflow, though it is not trade at all.

The trade balance is exports of goods minus imports of goods. Many countries, Sri Lanka included, run a deficit in goods and cover it with services earnings and remittances. A persistent gap has to be financed by borrowing or investment from abroad.

example.title: Adding up a year of foreign currency flows (illustrative)
steps: Goods exports $13 bn, goods imports $19 bn: trade balance −$6 bn.
Net: about +$4 bn before debt payments and investment flows.

lens.local: Apparel and tea have long been Sri Lanka's largest goods exports. Worker remittances, mainly from the Gulf, and tourism are the other big earners of foreign currency.
lens.regional: India is a major exporter of IT and business services, Bangladesh's exports are dominated by garments, and Vietnam has become a large electronics exporter.
lens.global: China is the world's largest exporter of goods and the United States runs the largest trade deficit. Commodity exporters such as Saudi Arabia earn most of their income from oil.

en.takeaway: A country pays for imports with exports, services, remittances or borrowing; when those inflows fall short, its currency comes under pressure.
sources: Central Bank of Sri Lanka: external sector statistics
World Trade Organization: trade statistics
World Bank: migration and remittances data

en.title: South Asia's economies at a glance
objectives: Name the main economies of South Asia and their strengths
Compare size with income per person
Explain how the region is linked to Sri Lanka
en.hook: Sri Lanka's biggest source of tourists, its largest supplier of imports and a key partner in its ports all sit within a short flight. Which economies are they?

sections.body: South Asia includes India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bhutan, the Maldives and Afghanistan. It is home to about a quarter of the world's people, and India alone produces roughly four-fifths of the region's output.

India has grown on services, manufacturing and a huge domestic market. Bangladesh built a garment export industry, the Maldives depends on tourism and Nepal on remittances. Sri Lanka has had among the highest incomes per person in the region, though its 2022 crisis set it back.

Trade within South Asia is low compared with East Asia, held back by tariffs, weak transport links and politics. The South Asian Free Trade Area (SAFTA) aimed to cut tariffs, and countries also have bilateral deals such as the India–Sri Lanka Free Trade Agreement.

example.title: Size versus income per person (illustrative, US dollars)
steps: Country A: GDP $80 bn, population 22 million → about $3,600 per person.
Country B: GDP $3,500 bn, population 1,400 million → about $2,500 per person.
Country B's economy is over 40 times larger.
Yet Country A's people have a higher average income.

lens.local: India is Sri Lanka's largest source of imports and of tourists, and Indian companies invest in Sri Lankan energy, ports and retail.
lens.regional: The Asian Development Bank, based in Manila, is a major lender to South Asian governments for roads, power and water projects.
lens.global: International forecasters such as the IMF and World Bank expect South Asia to remain one of the fastest-growing regions in the world, mainly because of India.

en.takeaway: South Asia is dominated by India, and Sri Lanka's trade, tourism and investment are closely tied to its neighbour.
sources: World Bank: South Asia economic updates
Asian Development Bank: Asian Development Outlook
IMF: Regional Economic Outlook, Asia and Pacific

en.title: Global institutions: IMF, World Bank, WTO
objectives: Explain what the IMF, World Bank and WTO each do
Describe when and how a country uses an IMF programme
Tell the three institutions apart
en.hook: In March 2023 the IMF approved a programme of about $3 billion for Sri Lanka. What is the IMF, and why do countries in crisis turn to it?

sections.body: The International Monetary Fund, created at Bretton Woods in 1944, watches over the world's monetary system. It lends to countries that cannot pay for imports or service their debts, usually on condition that they carry out reforms such as raising revenue or letting the exchange rate adjust. It also publishes forecasts and country reports.

The World Bank lends and gives grants for long-term development: roads, schools, health systems and power. Its arm for the poorest countries, the International Development Association, lends on very cheap terms. Where the IMF deals with balance-of-payments crises, the World Bank focuses on long-run growth and poverty.

The World Trade Organization, set up in 1995, sets the rules for trade between its members and settles disputes. Members agree to cut tariffs and treat each other's goods fairly. It does not lend money.

example.title: How an IMF programme works
steps: A country runs short of foreign currency and cannot pay its debts.
It agrees a programme with the IMF: targets for revenue, reserves and inflation.
The IMF releases money in instalments after regular reviews.
Other lenders often wait for the IMF's approval before lending or restructuring debt.

lens.local: Sri Lanka joined the IMF in 1950 and has used many programmes since; the one approved in 2023 was its seventeenth.
lens.regional: Thailand, Indonesia and South Korea borrowed from the IMF during the 1997 Asian financial crisis. Pakistan and Bangladesh have had recent programmes too.
lens.global: The IMF is funded by quotas from its 190-plus member countries, and the United States holds the largest share of votes. By tradition the World Bank's president has been American and the IMF's head European.

en.takeaway: The IMF handles short-term crises, the World Bank funds long-term development, and the WTO writes the trade rules.
sources: IMF: Sri Lanka Extended Fund Facility documents
World Bank: about the World Bank Group
World Trade Organization: what is the WTO

en.title: Budgeting and saving
objectives: Build a simple monthly budget
Explain why to save first and build an emergency fund
Compare saving habits across countries
en.hook: Two colleagues earn the same Rs 150,000 a month. One always runs short before payday; the other saves Rs 30,000. The difference is rarely income. It is a plan.

sections.body: A budget starts with knowing where money goes. Write down a month of spending and sort it into needs (rent, food, transport, loan payments), wants (eating out, subscriptions) and savings. Then set a limit for each group for the next month.

Move savings out of your account on payday, before spending, rather than saving whatever is left at the end. A common guide is 50% for needs, 30% for wants and 20% for saving, adjusted to your situation.

Keep three to six months of essential costs in a safe, easy-to-reach account. It stops a job loss or a hospital bill from turning into expensive debt. Only once it is in place should you take investment risk.

example.title: A Rs 150,000 monthly budget
steps: Emergency fund goal: 4 months × Rs 80,000 = Rs 320,000, reached in about 11 months.

lens.local: Many Sri Lankan households keep savings in fixed deposits, savings accounts and gold jewellery. Private-sector employees also save through the Employees' Provident Fund (EPF), with contributions deducted from salary and added by the employer.
lens.regional: Household saving rates in China and India have been high by world standards, partly because public pensions and health cover are limited.
lens.global: Many US households carry credit card debt and save little. The 50/30/20 rule of thumb was popularised there by Elizabeth Warren and Amelia Warren Tyagi.

en.takeaway: Save first, spend second, and build an emergency fund before you invest.
sources: Central Bank of Sri Lanka: Employees' Provident Fund
Elizabeth Warren and Amelia Warren Tyagi, All Your Worth (2005)

en.title: Deposits, loans and interest
objectives: Explain how banks use deposits to make loans
Calculate simple interest on a deposit and a loan
Compare deposit protection across countries
en.hook: Your bank pays you 7% on a fixed deposit and charges a business 12% on a loan. That gap is how most banks earn their living.

sections.body: Banks take deposits from savers and lend to households and businesses. They pay depositors interest, charge borrowers more, and keep the difference, called the net interest margin, to cover costs, bad loans and profit.

Current accounts are for everyday payments and usually pay no interest. Savings accounts pay a little and let you withdraw at any time. Fixed deposits pay more but lock money away for a set term, such as 3, 6 or 12 months.

A loan's rate depends on the bank's own cost of funds, the borrower's risk and any security offered. Rates can be fixed for the life of the loan or float with a benchmark. Compare the full cost, including fees, not just the headline rate.

example.title: One year of simple interest (illustrative)
steps: Fixed deposit: Rs 500,000 at 7% earns Rs 35,000.
Loan: Rs 500,000 at 12% costs the borrower Rs 60,000.
The bank's margin on that money: Rs 25,000 before costs.
If 2% of the loan goes bad, Rs 10,000 of that margin is lost.

lens.local: The Sri Lanka Deposit Insurance Scheme, run by the Central Bank, covers deposits at licensed banks and finance companies up to a set limit per depositor.
lens.regional: In India, the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation covers up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank.
lens.global: In the United States the FDIC insures up to $250,000 per depositor per bank; in the European Union the guarantee is €100,000.

en.takeaway: Banks earn the gap between what they pay savers and charge borrowers, and deposit insurance protects small savers if a bank fails.
sources: Central Bank of Sri Lanka: Sri Lanka Deposit Insurance Scheme
DICGC, India
US Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation

en.title: Simple and compound interest
objectives: Tell simple and compound interest apart
Calculate compound growth
Use the rule of 72
en.hook: Rs 100,000 saved at 10% a year becomes about Rs 260,000 in ten years, not Rs 200,000. The extra Rs 60,000 is interest earned on interest.

sections.body: Simple interest is paid only on the original amount. Rs 100,000 at 10% earns Rs 10,000 every year, so after ten years you have Rs 200,000.

Compound interest is paid on the original amount plus the interest already earned. Each year's interest is added to the balance and earns interest itself. The formula is: future value = amount × (1 + rate) raised to the number of years.
Divide 72 by the interest rate to estimate how many years money takes to double. At 8% it doubles in about 9 years; at 12%, in about 6. Starting early matters more than saving large amounts later.

example.title: Rs 100,000 at 10% a year, compounded annually
steps: Simple interest would have given Rs 200,000.

lens.local: Sri Lankan deposit rates are often several points higher than in rich countries, so compounding works fast, but so does inflation. Always compare the rate with inflation.
lens.regional: India's Public Provident Fund compounds interest every year over a 15-year term, a popular way to save for the long run.
lens.global: Albert Einstein is often quoted as calling compound interest the eighth wonder of the world, though there is no evidence he said it.

en.takeaway: Compounding rewards time: the earlier you start, the less you need to save.
sources: Any introductory finance textbook, time value of money chapter
National Savings Institute, India: Public Provident Fund

en.title: What a bond is: coupon, maturity, face value
objectives: Explain what a bond is and how it differs from a share
Identify face value, coupon and maturity
Compare government bond markets
en.hook: When the Sri Lankan government needs to borrow for ten years, it sells Treasury bonds to banks, pension funds and individuals. What exactly are they buying?

sections.body: A bond is a loan you make to a government or company. In return the issuer promises to pay regular interest and repay the original amount on a set date. Unlike a share, a bond does not make you an owner.

Face value is the amount repaid at the end, often Rs 100 per unit. The coupon is the yearly interest as a percentage of face value: a 10% coupon on Rs 100 pays Rs 10 a year, usually in two payments. Maturity is the date the face value is repaid.

Government debt of under a year is usually called a bill; it pays no coupon and is sold at a discount. Longer debt is a bond. Government bonds in a country's own currency are usually its safest investments, while company bonds pay more because they carry more risk.

example.title: A 5-year bond with a 10% coupon
steps: Coupon: 10% a year, paid as Rs 50,000 every six months.
At maturity, the Rs 1,000,000 face value is repaid.

lens.local: Sri Lanka's Treasury bonds pay coupons twice a year and are issued through auctions run by the Central Bank's Public Debt Department.
lens.regional: India's government securities market is one of the largest in Asia, and China's bond market is the second-largest in the world.
lens.global: US Treasury bonds are the world's benchmark safe asset. Their yields influence borrowing costs almost everywhere.

en.takeaway: A bond is a loan on a fixed schedule: coupons along the way and the face value at the end.
sources: Central Bank of Sri Lanka: Public Debt Department
Bank for International Settlements: debt securities statistics

en.title: Reading an income statement
objectives: Identify the main lines of an income statement
Calculate gross, operating and net margins
Know which reporting standards companies use
en.hook: A listed company announces revenue up 20%. Is that good news? Not until you have read the rest of the income statement.

sections.body: The income statement shows a company's performance over a period. It starts with revenue (sales), subtracts the cost of sales to give gross profit, then subtracts operating costs to give operating profit. After interest and tax comes net profit, the bottom line.

Margins turn profits into percentages of revenue, so companies of different sizes can be compared. Gross margin shows pricing power, operating margin shows how well the business is run, and net margin shows what is left for shareholders.
Net profit divided by the number of shares gives earnings per share (EPS). EPS growth over several years tells you more than any single quarter.

example.title: A simple income statement (Rs millions, illustrative)
steps: Revenue 1,000; cost of sales 600; gross profit 400, a 40% margin.
Operating costs 250; operating profit 150, a 15% margin.
Interest 30 and tax 36; net profit 84, an 8.4% margin.

lens.local: Companies listed on the Colombo Stock Exchange publish quarterly results under Sri Lanka Accounting Standards (SLFRS), which follow international standards.
lens.regional: Indian listed companies report under Ind AS, which is based on international standards. Compare margins rather than raw rupee figures across countries.
lens.global: Most countries use International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS), while US companies use US GAAP. The main lines look similar, but some items are treated differently.

en.takeaway: Revenue is only the start; margins and earnings per share show whether growth is turning into profit.
sources: CA Sri Lanka: Sri Lanka Accounting Standards
IFRS Foundation
Colombo Stock Exchange: listed company disclosures

en.title: Digital payments: LankaQR, India's UPI, cards
objectives: Explain how card, QR and instant payments work
Compare national payment systems
Use digital payments safely
en.hook: A tea stall in Galle, a vegetable seller in Chennai and a café in London can all be paid without cash in seconds. The systems behind them are very different.

sections.body: When you pay by card, QR code or app, no money physically moves. Your bank instructs the merchant's bank to credit their account, and the banks settle with each other through a payment network. Instant payment systems do this in seconds, around the clock.

Card payments run on networks such as Visa and Mastercard and charge merchants a fee. QR payments use a code the customer scans with a banking or wallet app, often at lower cost. Mobile wallets hold value or link to a bank account.
Fraudsters rarely break the technology; they trick people. Never share a one-time password, check the merchant's name before confirming, use official apps only, and turn on transaction alerts.

example.title: What payment fees mean for a shop (illustrative rates)
steps: Moving those sales to QR saves Rs 30,000 a month.

lens.local: LankaQR is Sri Lanka's national QR standard, run by LankaPay, which also operates the shared ATM and instant transfer networks.
lens.regional: India's Unified Payments Interface (UPI), launched in 2016, handles more than ten billion transactions a month and has been linked with payment systems in several countries, including Sri Lanka.
lens.global: Brazil's central bank launched the Pix instant payment system in 2020 and it spread rapidly. In the US and Europe, cards still dominate, though instant payments are growing.

en.takeaway: Digital payments move money between bank accounts in seconds; the technology is safe, so guard your codes.
sources: LankaPay: LankaQR
National Payments Corporation of India: UPI statistics
Banco Central do Brasil: Pix

en.title: What a market and an exchange are
objectives: Explain how buyers and sellers set a price
Describe what an exchange adds to a market
Tell primary and secondary markets apart
en.hook: At the Pettah wholesale market, onion prices change by the hour. At the Colombo Stock Exchange, share prices do the same, for the same reason.

sections.body: A market is any place, physical or online, where buyers and sellers meet. When more people want to buy than sell at the current price, the price rises; when sellers outnumber buyers, it falls. The price settles where the quantities match.

An exchange is an organised market with rules. It lists approved securities, matches buy and sell orders electronically, publishes prices so everyone sees the same information, and makes sure trades are settled. That trust lets strangers trade large amounts safely.

When a company or government sells new shares or bonds to raise money, that is the primary market. When investors later trade those securities among themselves, that is the secondary market. Most daily trading on an exchange is secondary, so the company receives no new money.

example.title: How orders set a price (illustrative)
steps: Buyers want 1,000 shares at Rs 50 and 2,000 at Rs 49.
Sellers offer 1,500 shares at Rs 50 and 3,000 at Rs 51.
Rs 50 becomes the last traded price that everyone sees.

lens.local: The Colombo Stock Exchange took its current form in 1985 and lists close to 300 companies.
lens.regional: India's National Stock Exchange is one of the busiest exchanges in the world by number of trades, especially in derivatives.
lens.global: The New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq are the largest stock exchanges by the value of listed companies. London's exchange grew out of coffee-house trading in the late 1600s.

en.takeaway: Prices are set by the balance of buyers and sellers; an exchange makes that process fair, visible and safe.
sources: Colombo Stock Exchange: about the CSE
World Federation of Exchanges: market statistics

en.title: Exchanges compared: CSE, NSE, NYSE, LSE
objectives: Describe how individuals access an exchange
Compare major exchanges by size, hours and settlement
Explain what a CDS account is
en.hook: A Sri Lankan investor can buy shares in Colombo before lunch, watch Mumbai close in the afternoon and see New York open in the evening. How do these exchanges compare?

sections.body: Individuals cannot trade directly on an exchange. You open an account with a licensed stockbroker, who sends your orders to the exchange. Your shares are held electronically in a central depository rather than as paper certificates.

Each exchange trades during set hours in its own time zone. Settlement is when money and shares actually change hands; many markets now settle one or two business days after the trade. Fees include brokerage commission and charges from the exchange, the depository and the regulator.

Exchanges differ hugely in size. A market with many large companies and heavy trading lets investors buy and sell quickly at close to the quoted price. In smaller markets, a modest order can move the price a lot.

example.title: Four exchanges at a glance
steps: CSE, Colombo: 9:30 am to 2:30 pm Sri Lanka time; close to 300 listed companies.
NSE, Mumbai: 9:15 am to 3:30 pm India time, the same clock as Colombo; over 2,000 listed companies.
NYSE, New York: 9:30 am to 4:00 pm US Eastern time, which is evening in Colombo.
LSE, London: 8:00 am to 4:30 pm UK time.

lens.local: To trade on the CSE you need a Central Depository System (CDS) account, opened through a licensed stockbroker; many brokers now offer online account opening.
lens.regional: In India, shares are held in demat accounts with the depositories NSDL or CDSL, and India completed the move to next-day (T+1) settlement in 2023.
lens.global: The US moved to T+1 settlement in May 2024. In London, the Main Market serves larger companies and AIM serves smaller growth companies.

en.takeaway: Every exchange works the same way at heart, through a broker, a depository and a settlement cycle, but size, hours and costs differ widely.
sources: Colombo Stock Exchange: how to invest
Securities and Exchange Board of India: T+1 settlement
US SEC: shortening the settlement cycle

en.title: Government bills and bonds
objectives: Explain why governments borrow in the market
Describe how an auction sets yields
Show how bill yields reach bank rates
en.hook: Every week the Central Bank announces the results of a Treasury bill auction. A small change in those yields can move fixed deposit rates within weeks.

sections.h: Why governments borrow in the market
sections.body: Governments borrow to cover budget deficits and to repay old debt as it matures. Selling bills and bonds to banks, funds and individuals lets them borrow in their own currency at market rates rather than printing money.

The government announces how much it wants to borrow and for how long. Bidders say how much they will lend and at what yield. The government accepts the cheapest bids first until it has raised what it needs, and the accepted yields become the market's benchmark.

sections.h: Why bill yields matter to you
sections.body: Short-term government yields are the base on which banks price deposits and loans. When bill yields fall, fixed deposit and loan rates usually follow, and the same happens in reverse.

example.title: Buying a 364-day Treasury bill (illustrative)
steps: At maturity you receive Rs 1,000,000, a gain of Rs 74,074.

lens.local: Sri Lanka auctions Treasury bills of 91, 182 and 364 days every week, and Treasury bonds less often, through the Central Bank's Public Debt Department and licensed primary dealers.
lens.regional: The Reserve Bank of India runs auctions for Indian government securities, and Indian government bonds joined major global bond indices in 2024.
lens.global: The US Treasury auctions bills every week and is the largest government borrower in the world.

en.takeaway: Government auctions set a country's benchmark interest rates, which flow through to the rates you get at the bank.
sources: Central Bank of Sri Lanka: Treasury bill auction results
Reserve Bank of India: government securities market
US Treasury: auctions

en.title: How exchange rates are quoted
objectives: Read an exchange rate quote
Tell buying and selling rates apart
Explain appreciation and depreciation
en.hook: A board at the bank says USD 296 / 304. Which number do you get when you change your dollars, and which do you pay?

sections.body: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in another. USD/LKR 300 means one US dollar costs 300 rupees. The first currency is the base and the second is the quote currency; a higher number means the base currency is stronger.

Banks and money changers quote two prices. The buying rate is what they pay you for foreign currency; the selling rate is what they charge you. The gap, the spread, is their margin, so compare spreads, not just one rate.

When USD/LKR rises from 300 to 320, the rupee has depreciated: it takes more rupees to buy a dollar. When it falls to 290, the rupee has appreciated. A weaker currency helps exporters and hurts importers.

example.title: Changing $1,000 at the counter (illustrative)
steps: Bank buying rate Rs 296: you receive Rs 296,000.
Buying the $1,000 back would cost Rs 304,000.
The round trip costs you Rs 8,000.

lens.local: The Central Bank publishes a daily indicative US dollar rate, and banks set their own buying and selling rates around it. The rupee floats, and the Central Bank can buy or sell dollars to smooth sharp moves.
lens.regional: Most Asian currencies are quoted against the dollar: USD/INR for the Indian rupee and USD/CNY for China's yuan, which China manages within a band around a daily reference rate.
lens.global: The most traded currency pair in the world is EUR/USD. By convention the euro and the British pound are quoted as the base currency against the dollar.

en.takeaway: An exchange rate is a price; check which currency is the base, and always compare the spread.
sources: Central Bank of Sri Lanka: exchange rates
Bank for International Settlements: Triennial Survey of foreign exchange

en.title: Oil, gold and tea prices
objectives: Explain how commodity prices are set
Name the main price benchmarks
Trace how a price change reaches Sri Lanka
en.hook: When oil prices jump, Sri Lanka's fuel prices, bus fares and electricity costs follow. When tea prices rise at the Colombo auction, estates across the hill country breathe easier.

sections.body: Commodities are raw materials traded in standard grades, so one barrel of a given oil grade is the same as another. Prices are set globally by supply and demand and, for most commodities, quoted in US dollars.

Brent crude, from the North Sea, is the main global oil benchmark, and West Texas Intermediate is the US one. Gold is priced per troy ounce in London and New York. Tea is sold at auctions, and Colombo runs one of the largest in the world.

Weather, wars, decisions by oil producers in OPEC+ and the strength of the US dollar all move commodity prices. Because new supply takes years to arrive, prices can rise or fall sharply within months.

example.title: How an oil price rise reaches the pump (illustrative)
steps: Brent rises from $70 to $84 a barrel, up 20%.
Crude is only part of the pump price; taxes, refining and transport make up the rest.
If crude is half the pump price, pump prices rise about 10%.
Sri Lanka's monthly fuel pricing formula passes such changes on to consumers.

lens.local: The Colombo Tea Auction, held weekly since 1883, sets prices for most of Sri Lanka's tea. Sri Lanka imports all of its crude oil and refined fuel.
lens.regional: India is one of the world's largest importers of both oil and gold, and Indian demand for gold jewellery peaks in the wedding and festival seasons.
lens.global: OPEC+ groups major producers including Saudi Arabia and Russia and can move prices by changing output. Central banks have been large buyers of gold in recent years.

en.takeaway: Commodity prices are set globally in dollars, so Sri Lanka feels every swing in oil, gold and tea through its import bill and exports.
sources: Colombo Tea Traders' Association: auction reports
OPEC: Monthly Oil Market Report
World Gold Council: gold demand trends

en.title: Spotting scams and pyramid schemes
objectives: Recognise the warning signs of investment fraud
Explain why pyramid and Ponzi schemes collapse
Know how to check a firm before paying
en.hook: A friend says her investment club pays 10% a month, and you earn more for every new member you bring. It sounds too good to be true. It is.

sections.body: Guaranteed high returns, pressure to act fast, rewards for recruiting others, vague explanations of how money is made, and requests to pay in cash or crypto are all red flags. Real investments carry risk and do not promise fixed high returns.

A pyramid scheme pays early members out of new members' joining fees. A Ponzi scheme pays returns to existing investors out of new investors' money. Both need ever more newcomers, so they always collapse, and most people lose their money.
Ask whether the firm is licensed by the regulator and look it up on the regulator's website. Never invest in something you cannot explain, and never pay into a personal account.

example.title: Why a pyramid must collapse
steps: Each member must recruit 6 new members.
Level 10 would need over 60 million people.
Long before that, recruitment stops and the scheme collapses.

lens.local: The Central Bank of Sri Lanka has named a number of entities as prohibited schemes under the Banking Act and publishes warnings about unauthorised deposit-taking.
lens.regional: India's Saradha scheme collapsed in 2013, costing large numbers of small savers in West Bengal and nearby states their money.
lens.global: Bernie Madoff ran the largest known Ponzi scheme in US history, with paper losses of around $65 billion, until his arrest in 2008.

en.takeaway: If returns are guaranteed and high, or you are paid to recruit, walk away and check with the regulator.
sources: Central Bank of Sri Lanka: prohibited schemes
Securities and Exchange Commission of Sri Lanka: investor alerts
US SEC: Ponzi schemes

en.title: Saving vs investing; goals and time horizons
objectives: Tell saving and investing apart
Match money to goals and time horizons
Explain why inflation matters for long-term money
en.hook: Kasun is saving for a motorbike next year and for retirement in 30 years. Should both pots of money be in the same place?

sections.body: Saving means keeping money safe and available, usually in a bank. Investing means buying assets such as shares, bonds, funds or property that are expected to grow over time, accepting that their value will rise and fall along the way.

Start with the goal and when you will need the money. Money needed within one or two years belongs somewhere safe, such as a deposit or Treasury bills. Money for goals five or more years away can take more risk, because there is time to recover from falls.

Over long periods, cash in the bank often barely keeps up with inflation. Investments with higher expected returns, such as shares, have historically beaten inflation over decades, but with large ups and downs.

example.title: Two goals, two plans (illustrative)
steps: Motorbike in 12 months, Rs 600,000: Rs 50,000 a month into a fixed deposit.
Retirement in 30 years: Rs 10,000 a month into a diversified fund.
At an assumed 10% a year, the retirement pot grows to about Rs 22.6 million.
Of that, only Rs 3.6 million is money paid in; the rest is growth.

lens.local: Sri Lankan savers have long relied on fixed deposits, gold and land. Unit trusts and the stock market offer other ways to invest for long-term goals.
lens.regional: In India, millions of people invest a fixed sum in mutual funds every month through systematic investment plans (SIPs).
lens.global: In the United States, workplace retirement accounts such as 401(k) plans are the main way most people invest, often in low-cost index funds.

en.takeaway: Match the money to the goal: safe places for near goals, growth investments for distant ones.
sources: Securities and Exchange Commission of Sri Lanka: investor education
Association of Mutual Funds in India: SIP data

en.title: Reading a stock quote
objectives: Read each part of a stock quote
Explain volume and market capitalisation
Compare quotes across exchanges
en.hook: A screen shows COMB.N0000 148.75 ▲ 2.75 (1.88%) Vol 4.1m. In five seconds you should know what every part means.

sections.body: A quote shows the ticker symbol, the last traded price, the change from the previous close (in money and percent), and the day's high, low and volume. The bid is the best price buyers are offering; the ask is the best price sellers want.
Volume is the number of shares traded. High volume means it is easy to buy or sell without moving the price, while a big move on low volume can reverse quickly.

Market capitalisation is the share price multiplied by the number of shares in issue. It shows the company's size as the market values it, and indices such as the ASPI, Nifty 50 and S&P 500 weight their members by it.

example.title: Working out a company's size (illustrative)
steps: At Rs 300 to the dollar, that is about $645 million.

lens.local: On the CSE, the ticker suffix matters: .N0000 marks voting ordinary shares and .X0000 non-voting shares, which often trade at a lower price.
lens.regional: Indian shares often trade on both the NSE and the BSE, so the same company can show slightly different prices on each at the same moment.
lens.global: US tickers are short codes such as AAPL for Apple. Prices are in dollars, and many US shares also trade before and after official hours.

en.takeaway: Read price, change and volume together, and use market capitalisation to judge a company's size.
sources: Colombo Stock Exchange: market information
National Stock Exchange of India: market data

en.title: Buying bills and bonds as an individual
objectives: Describe the ways individuals can buy government securities
Calculate the return on a Treasury bill
Know the risks that remain
en.hook: Treasury bills often pay more than a savings account and are backed by the government. Yet most people have never bought one. How do you?

sections.body: Individuals can buy government bills and bonds through primary dealers and many commercial banks, which bid in auctions or sell from their own holdings. Some countries let individuals bid directly online, and money-market and gilt funds offer an indirect route.

A bill's return is the gap between the price you pay and the face value you receive. A bond pays coupons and returns its face value at maturity. Sell a bond before maturity and you get the market price, which may be above or below what you paid.
Local-currency government securities carry a very low risk of non-payment, but they still face inflation risk and, for bonds sold early, price risk when interest rates rise.

example.title: Return on a 182-day bill (illustrative)
steps: Price paid: Rs 961,000 for Rs 1,000,000 of face value.
Gain: Rs 39,000 over about six months.

lens.local: In Sri Lanka, individuals can buy Treasury bills and bonds through licensed primary dealers and many banks. In the 2023 domestic debt restructuring, bonds held by pension funds such as the EPF were exchanged for new ones; other holders were not required to take part.
lens.regional: India's RBI Retail Direct, launched in 2021, lets individuals open an account with the central bank and bid for government securities online.
lens.global: In the United States, individuals can buy Treasuries directly from the government through TreasuryDirect, with no fees.

en.takeaway: Government bills and bonds are among the safest ways to earn interest, and individuals can buy them through dealers, banks or direct schemes.
sources: Central Bank of Sri Lanka: Public Debt Department
Reserve Bank of India: RBI Retail Direct
US Treasury: TreasuryDirect

en.title: Unit trusts and mutual funds
objectives: Explain how a fund pools money
Read a fund's unit price and fees
Compare the main types of fund
en.hook: With Rs 10,000 you cannot buy shares in 30 companies. With a unit trust, you can own a small slice of all of them.

sections.body: A unit trust or mutual fund pools money from many investors, and a professional manager invests it in shares, bonds or deposits. Each investor owns units. The value of a unit, the net asset value (NAV), is the fund's total assets divided by the number of units.

Money-market funds hold short-term deposits and bills and aim for stability. Income or gilt funds hold bonds. Equity funds hold shares and aim for long-term growth with bigger swings. Balanced funds mix the two.

Funds charge a yearly management fee, and some charge entry or exit fees. Paying 2% a year instead of 1% can cut the final value of a long-term investment by a large amount, so compare fees and past performance after fees.

example.title: Buying units (illustrative)
steps: You invest Rs 100,000 and receive 4,000 units.
A year later the NAV is Rs 27.50, so your units are worth Rs 110,000.
Your return is 10%, after the fund's fees have been taken from its assets.

lens.local: Unit trusts in Sri Lanka are licensed by the Securities and Exchange Commission of Sri Lanka, and their trustees are usually banks.
lens.regional: India's mutual fund industry has grown rapidly under the supervision of SEBI, with many investors paying in monthly through SIPs.
lens.global: In the United States, mutual funds and ETFs hold trillions of dollars, and the shift to low-cost index funds has pushed fees down worldwide.

en.takeaway: A fund gives you instant diversification and professional management; check what it holds and what it charges.
sources: Securities and Exchange Commission of Sri Lanka: unit trusts
Unit Trust Association of Sri Lanka
Investment Company Institute: fact book

en.title: Diversification
objectives: Explain why spreading money reduces risk
Diversify across companies, sectors, assets and countries
Spot false diversification
en.hook: In 2022, investors who held only rupee assets saw their buying power fall sharply as the rupee weakened and prices soared. Those who had spread their money were hit far less.

sections.body: Different investments rise and fall at different times. When one company, sector or country has a bad year, others may do well. Holding a mix smooths the ride without necessarily lowering the long-run return.

Spread across companies (many shares, not one), across sectors (banks, consumer goods, plantations, technology), across asset types (shares, bonds, cash, property) and across countries and currencies. Each layer protects against a different kind of shock.
Owning ten banks is not diversification, because banks tend to move together. Nor is owning several funds that all hold the same large companies. Check what you actually own underneath.

example.title: One share versus ten (illustrative)
steps: Rs 1,000,000 in one company that falls 50%: you lose Rs 500,000.
Rs 100,000 in each of ten companies, one falls 50%, the rest are flat.
Diversification turned a disaster into a setback.

lens.local: The CSE is small and concentrated in a few sectors such as banking and diversified holding companies, so local shares alone offer limited diversification.
lens.regional: Asian markets often move differently from each other: in some years India rises while China falls, so holding several reduces risk.
lens.global: Global index funds hold thousands of companies in dozens of countries, the broadest diversification open to small investors.

en.takeaway: Don't put everything in one share, sector, asset or country, and check that your holdings don't all move together.
sources: Securities and Exchange Commission of Sri Lanka: investor education
Any introductory investments textbook, portfolio theory chapter

en.title: Why invest abroad
objectives: Explain the benefits of investing outside your home market
Describe the extra risks, especially currency risk
Know the main routes abroad
en.hook: The whole Colombo Stock Exchange is worth far less than a single large US technology company. An investor who stays local misses most of the world's companies.

sections.body: Most of the world's companies, industries and growth are outside any one country. Investing abroad gives access to sectors your home market lacks, such as large technology or healthcare firms, and spreads risk across economies and currencies.

Foreign investments carry currency risk: if the foreign currency weakens against yours, your return shrinks, and the reverse. There are also different tax rules, higher costs, time-zone gaps and less familiarity with the companies.

Investors can buy foreign shares through international brokers where rules allow, buy local funds that invest overseas, or buy global index funds and ETFs. Each country's foreign exchange rules decide what is permitted.

example.title: How the currency changes your return (illustrative)
steps: You invest $1,000 when USD/LKR is 300: Rs 300,000.
If the rupee weakens to 330, that is Rs 363,000, a 21% gain in rupees.
If it strengthens to 270, it is Rs 297,000, a 1% loss.

lens.local: Sri Lankans' ability to move money abroad for investment is governed by the Foreign Exchange Act and Central Bank directions, which were tightened during the 2022 crisis.
lens.regional: India's Liberalised Remittance Scheme lets residents send up to $250,000 a year abroad, including for investment.
lens.global: Investors everywhere tend to hold mostly home-country assets, a pattern called home bias, even though their home market is a small share of the world.

en.takeaway: Investing abroad widens your choice and spreads risk, but adds currency risk and depends on your country's rules.
sources: Central Bank of Sri Lanka: Foreign Exchange Act directions
Reserve Bank of India: Liberalised Remittance Scheme

en.title: Common investor mistakes
objectives: Recognise the most common investing mistakes
Explain why they happen
Use simple rules to avoid them
en.hook: During a rally, everyone at the office talks about shares. After a fall, nobody does. Many people buy at the first moment and sell at the second.

sections.body: Buying something because its price has already shot up is the most common mistake. Last year's best performer is often not next year's, and late buyers carry the risk of a fall.
Selling after a big fall locks in the loss and often misses the recovery. Markets have recovered from many deep falls over time, though not always quickly.

Putting most of your money into one tip, one company or one sector risks a large loss. Trading often adds brokerage fees and taxes and usually lowers returns. A plan, a diversified portfolio and patience beat most short-term bets.

example.title: The cost of missing a recovery (illustrative)
steps: You invest Rs 1,000,000 and the market falls 30% to Rs 700,000.
You sell in panic and hold cash.
Over the next two years the market rises 50%.
Holding on would have given Rs 1,050,000; selling left Rs 700,000 plus a little interest.

lens.local: The CSE has seen sharp booms, including in 2010 and 2021, each followed by falls, and many new investors joined near the top.
lens.regional: In India, a surge of new retail traders after 2020 was followed by heavy losses in options; a SEBI study found that most individual derivatives traders lost money.
lens.global: Research on US investors by Brad Barber and Terrance Odean found that those who traded the most earned the lowest returns.

en.takeaway: Most investing mistakes come from emotion; a written plan and diversification protect you from yourself.
sources: SEBI: study of individual traders in equity derivatives
Barber and Odean, Trading Is Hazardous to Your Wealth (2000)

en.prompt: What does real GDP remove from the figures?
en.explain: Real GDP strips out inflation, so it shows changes in actual output.

en.prompt: Real GDP rises from Rs 200 trillion to Rs 210 trillion. What is the growth rate, in %?
GDP includes unpaid work done at home.
en.explain: Unpaid household work is not sold in a market, so GDP leaves it out.

en.prompt: What does a consumer price index track?
options: The prices of a basket of goods and services households buy
Share prices on the stock exchange
en.explain: A CPI follows the cost of a fixed, weighted basket of household purchases.

en.prompt: A price index rises from 150 to 162 over a year. What is inflation, in %?
Which index does the Central Bank of Sri Lanka use for its inflation target?
en.explain: The Central Bank targets inflation measured by the Colombo Consumer Price Index.

en.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the three jobs of money?
en.explain: Money is a medium of exchange, a unit of account and a store of value. It guarantees no return.

en.prompt: Most money in a modern economy is bank deposits rather than notes and coins.
en.explain: Bank lending creates deposits, which make up most of the money people use.

en.prompt: What is the main objective of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka under its 2023 Act?
en.explain: The 2023 Act made domestic price stability the Central Bank's primary objective.

en.prompt: What is the primary balance?
options: Revenue minus spending, leaving out interest payments
en.explain: The primary balance excludes interest, so it shows whether current policy is adding to debt.

en.prompt: Revenue is Rs 5 trillion and spending excluding interest is Rs 4.6 trillion. What is the primary balance, in Rs trillion (a surplus is positive)?
en.explain: 5 − 4.6 = 0.4, a primary surplus of Rs 0.4 trillion.

en.prompt: Taxes on spending, such as VAT, take a bigger share of poorer households' income.
en.explain: Poorer households spend a larger share of their income, so spending taxes weigh more on them.

en.prompt: Which of these is an import for Sri Lanka?
options: An Indian tourist staying at a Kandy hotel
en.explain: Fuel bought from abroad is an import. Tourist spending and tea sales earn foreign currency, so they are exports.

en.prompt: Goods exports are $12 billion and goods imports $18 billion. What is the trade balance, in $ billion?
en.explain: 12 − 18 = −6, a trade deficit of $6 billion.

en.prompt: Remittances are a type of export.
en.explain: Remittances are transfers from people working abroad, not sales of goods or services.

en.prompt: Which country produces most of South Asia's output?

en.prompt: A country's GDP is $90 billion and its population 22.5 million. What is GDP per person, in US dollars?
Trade within South Asia is high compared with trade within East Asia.
en.explain: Intra-regional trade in South Asia is low, held back by tariffs, transport and politics.

en.prompt: Which institution lends to countries facing a balance-of-payments crisis?
options: The Asian Development Bank's trade office
en.explain: The IMF's main lending role is to help countries short of foreign currency.

en.prompt: What does the WTO mainly do?
options: Sets trade rules and settles disputes
en.explain: The WTO writes and enforces trade rules between its members; it does not lend.

en.prompt: IMF money is usually released all at once at the start of a programme.
en.explain: It is released in instalments after regular reviews of the programme's targets.

en.prompt: Your monthly income is Rs 120,000. Under the 50/30/20 rule, how much goes to savings, in Rs?
What should you build before taking investment risk?
en.explain: An emergency fund keeps a surprise bill from forcing you into debt or into selling investments.

en.prompt: Paying yourself first means saving whatever is left at the end of the month.
en.explain: It means moving savings aside on payday, before you spend.

en.prompt: A Rs 200,000 fixed deposit pays 8% for one year. How much interest does it earn, in Rs?
What is a bank's net interest margin?
options: The gap between interest earned on loans and paid on deposits
The fee for a cheque book
en.explain: It is the difference between what the bank earns on loans and pays to depositors.

en.prompt: US deposit insurance covers up to how much per depositor per bank?
en.explain: The FDIC insures up to $250,000 per depositor per bank.

en.explain: 72 ÷ 9 = 8 years.

Compound interest is paid on…
options: The original amount plus interest already earned
en.explain: Compounding means interest also earns interest.

en.prompt: A bond with Rs 100 face value has an 8% coupon. How much interest does it pay per year, in Rs?
en.explain: 8% of Rs 100 is Rs 8 a year.

en.prompt: What does a bondholder own?
options: A claim to interest and repayment
A vote at the annual meeting
en.explain: A bond is a loan, so it gives a claim to payments, not ownership.

en.prompt: A Treasury bill usually pays a coupon every six months.
en.explain: Bills pay no coupon; they are sold at a discount and repaid at face value.

en.prompt: Revenue is Rs 500 million and gross profit Rs 150 million. What is the gross margin, in %?
Which line is the bottom line?
en.explain: Net profit, after all costs, interest and tax, sits at the bottom of the statement.

en.prompt: Net profit is Rs 60 million and there are 120 million shares. What are earnings per share, in Rs?
en.explain: 60 ÷ 120 = Rs 0.50 per share.

en.explain: UPI was launched in India in 2016 by the National Payments Corporation of India.

It is safe to share your one-time password with someone who says they are from your bank.
en.explain: Banks never ask for your one-time password. Anyone who does is attempting fraud.

en.prompt: When you buy shares on the exchange from another investor, the company receives your money.

en.explain: Excess demand pushes the price up until buying and selling balance.

en.prompt: What is settlement?

When a company pays a dividend

en.prompt: Who sets the yield in a Treasury bill auction?
options: Bidders, through the rates they offer
en.explain: The government accepts the cheapest bids, so bidders' rates set the yield.

en.prompt: A one-year bill has a face value of Rs 100,000 and a yield of 10%. About what price do you pay, in Rs?
When Treasury bill yields fall, fixed deposit rates usually rise.
en.explain: Deposit rates usually follow bill yields in the same direction.

en.prompt: USD/LKR moves from 300 to 330. What happened to the rupee?
en.explain: It now takes more rupees to buy a dollar, so the rupee weakened.

en.prompt: The buying rate is 295 and the selling rate 303. What is the spread, in rupees?
Which currency pair is the most traded in the world?
en.explain: Euro against dollar is the largest currency market.

en.prompt: Which is the main global oil price benchmark?
en.explain: Brent crude is the most widely used oil benchmark.

en.prompt: Sri Lanka produces most of the crude oil it uses.
en.explain: Sri Lanka imports all of its crude oil and refined fuel.

Which of these is a warning sign of fraud?

en.explain: That is exactly how a Ponzi scheme works, which is why it collapses when new money dries up.

en.prompt: Before investing with a firm, you should…
options: Check that it is licensed by the regulator

en.title: Scarcity and choice
objectives: Define scarcity, choice and opportunity cost
Read and use a production possibilities frontier
Explain how economies decide what to produce, how and for whom

learn.body: Economics studies how people, firms and governments use scarce resources. Land, labour, machines and time are limited, but wants are not, so every decision means giving something up. A family in Kandy deciding how to spend a salary, a company in Colombo choosing where to invest and a government choosing between roads and hospitals all face the same problem.

The opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the best alternative you give up. If you spend Rs 50,000 on a phone instead of a course, the course is the opportunity cost. Time has an opportunity cost too: four hours of study could have been four hours of paid work. Good decisions compare opportunity costs, not just prices.

Economists group resources into four factors: land (natural resources such as tea land, minerals and the sea), labour (people's time and skills), capital (machines, buildings and roads) and entrepreneurship (organising the other three and taking risk). Each earns an income: rent, wages, interest and profit.

A production possibilities frontier (PPF) shows the most an economy can produce of two goods with its current resources and technology. Points on the curve are efficient. Points inside it mean resources are wasted, for example through unemployment. Points outside cannot be reached today. Moving along the curve shows the opportunity cost of making more of one good.

The frontier moves outward when an economy gains resources or better technology: a larger skilled workforce, new machinery, better roads or new ideas. It moves inward after disasters, conflict or a deep crisis. In this picture, economic growth is the frontier moving out over time.

Every economy answers three questions: what to produce, how to produce it and who gets it. Market economies answer mainly through prices and private choices; command economies through government plans. Most real economies, including Sri Lanka, India and the United States, are mixed: markets do most of the work while governments regulate, tax, provide services and support those in need.

Microeconomics studies individual decisions: households, firms and single markets such as rice or rental housing. Macroeconomics studies the whole economy: growth, inflation, unemployment, interest rates and trade. This programme starts with these micro foundations and moves to the big picture, because national outcomes are built from millions of individual choices.

en.title: Markets, supply and demand
objectives: Explain demand and supply and what shifts each
Find the equilibrium price and quantity
Analyse a real price change using supply and demand

learn.body: A market is any arrangement that lets buyers and sellers trade: the Dambulla wholesale market, a supermarket in Colombo, an online platform. Prices carry information. A rising price tells buyers a good has become scarce and tells producers it is worth supplying more.

Demand is how much buyers want to buy at each price. The law of demand says that, other things equal, a higher price means a lower quantity demanded, because people switch to substitutes and their money goes less far. On a graph, the demand curve slopes downward.

Demand shifts when something other than the good's own price changes: incomes, the prices of substitutes (chicken and fish) and complements (cars and fuel), tastes, population and expectations. A shift moves the whole curve; a change in the good's own price moves along it.

Supply is how much sellers offer at each price. Higher prices usually bring more supply, because producing more becomes profitable. Supply shifts with input costs such as fertiliser, fuel and wages, with technology, weather, taxes and the number of sellers.

The equilibrium price is where the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied. Above it, unsold goods pile up and sellers cut prices; below it, shortages appear and prices rise. Markets move towards equilibrium unless something stops them.

A price ceiling below equilibrium, such as a maximum retail price, creates shortages and queues. A price floor above equilibrium, such as a guaranteed paddy price, creates surpluses that the government may have to buy. Controls shift income between groups, but they also change how people behave.

Elasticity measures how strongly quantity responds to price. Rice and fuel have inelastic demand: people buy similar amounts even when prices rise. Goods with close substitutes are elastic. Elasticity decides how much a price rise changes spending and who carries the burden of a tax.

en.title: GDP and how it is measured
objectives: Define GDP and measure it three ways
Tell real from nominal GDP and calculate growth
Compare GDP across countries using exchange rates and PPP

learn.body: GDP is the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a period. Final means sold to the last user: counting flour sold to a bakery as well as the bread would count the flour twice. Within a country means production by foreign firms in Sri Lanka counts, while Sri Lankans' earnings abroad do not.

GDP equals consumption plus investment plus government spending plus exports minus imports: C + I + G + (X − M). Imports are subtracted because they were produced elsewhere. In most countries, household consumption is the largest part.

GDP can also be measured as total income earned (wages, profits, rent and interest, plus taxes on production) or as the value added by each sector: agriculture, industry and services. Value added is a firm's sales minus the cost of the inputs it bought.

Nominal GDP uses current prices, so it rises with inflation. Real GDP uses the prices of a base year, so it shows changes in the volume of output. The GDP deflator, nominal GDP divided by real GDP times 100, is a broad measure of price change.

The growth rate is the percentage change in real GDP from one period to the next. Quarterly figures are usually compared with the same quarter a year earlier, to remove seasonal patterns such as the tourist season or the Maha harvest.

To compare countries, GDP is converted into a common currency, usually US dollars. Market exchange rates can mislead because prices differ: a haircut costs far less in Colombo than in London. Purchasing power parity (PPP) adjusts for these price differences, so lower-income countries look relatively larger in PPP terms.

Gross national income (GNI) adds income residents earn from work and investment abroad and subtracts income paid to foreigners, such as profits sent home by foreign companies. Remittances from migrant workers are added in a wider measure, gross national disposable income. For Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh, that gap matters.

en.title: Growth, jobs and unemployment
objectives: Explain what drives long-run growth
Calculate unemployment and participation rates
Tell frictional, structural and cyclical unemployment apart

learn.body: Small differences in growth add up. At 2% a year, income doubles in about 35 years; at 7%, in about 10. South Korea, China and Vietnam raised living standards dramatically by sustaining fast growth for decades.

Output grows when an economy has more workers, more capital per worker, or better technology and organisation, which economists call productivity. Over the long run productivity matters most, because adding workers and machines alone runs into diminishing returns.

Education and skills, good infrastructure, openness to trade and ideas, stable prices, the rule of law and competition all raise productivity. Economies that kept these in place for decades, such as the East Asian economies, grew faster than those that did not.

The labour force is everyone working plus everyone actively looking for work. The unemployment rate is the unemployed divided by the labour force. The labour force participation rate is the labour force divided by the working-age population.

Frictional unemployment is the short gap between jobs. Structural unemployment comes from a mismatch between workers' skills or locations and the jobs available. Cyclical unemployment rises in recessions when demand falls. Each calls for a different response: better job matching, training, or support for demand.

Many workers in South Asia have informal jobs without contracts or social protection, or work fewer hours than they would like. A low unemployment rate can therefore hide poor job quality. Women's participation is a key issue: in Sri Lanka and India it is far below men's.

Many Sri Lankans, Nepalis and Bangladeshis work abroad, mostly in the Gulf, and send money home. Migration eases pressure on local job markets, but it can also drain skills when doctors, nurses and engineers leave.

en.title: Income, poverty and inequality
objectives: Measure poverty using poverty lines
Read a Gini coefficient and income shares
Explain policies that reduce poverty and inequality

learn.body: GDP per person is an average. A few very high incomes can lift it while most people see little change. To understand living standards we need to know how income is shared and how many people are poor.

A poverty line is the income or spending needed for a minimum standard of living. Sri Lanka's official line is set by the Department of Census and Statistics and updated for prices. For global comparisons the World Bank uses an extreme poverty line of $3.00 a day in 2021 PPP terms, raised in 2025 from $2.15.

The Gini coefficient runs from 0, where everyone has the same income, to 1, where one person has everything. Income shares are easier to read: what share goes to the richest 10% compared with the poorest 40%? A Lorenz curve shows the whole distribution.

South Africa and Brazil have among the highest measured inequality in the world, and the Nordic countries among the lowest. Measured inequality in South Asia is moderate, though household surveys often miss the very richest.

Differences in education, ownership of land and capital, gaps between regions such as the Western Province and the rest of the country, gender, and access to finance all shape inequality. Technology and globalisation tend to reward people with skills and capital.
Shocks fall hardest on households with no savings. World Bank estimates suggested Sri Lanka's poverty rate roughly doubled between 2021 and 2022, as food and fuel prices soared and incomes fell.

Targeted cash transfers, such as Sri Lanka's Aswesuma programme or India's direct benefit transfers, along with good public education and health, fair taxes and access to finance, reduce poverty and inequality. Targeting matters: support must reach those who need it most.

en.title: Sri Lanka's economy since 1948
objectives: Describe the main phases of Sri Lanka's economic policy since independence
Explain the causes of the 2022 crisis
Compare Sri Lanka's path with other Asian economies

learn.body: In 1948 Ceylon was a plantation economy exporting tea, rubber and coconut. It had high literacy and life expectancy for its income level. Early governments expanded free education, free health care and food subsidies, building strong social indicators.
Governments nationalised key industries, restricted imports and controlled prices to protect local producers. The early 1970s brought severe import controls and shortages, and growth was slow.

The 1977 reforms opened the economy: import controls were eased, the exchange rate was reformed, and export processing zones such as Katunayake attracted garment factories. Apparel grew to become the largest export industry.

The civil war cost many lives and deterred investment, yet the economy grew at around 5% a year on average, helped by garments, remittances and services. Heavy defence spending and persistent deficits pushed up public debt.

After the war ended in 2009, growth rose on large infrastructure projects, many financed by foreign borrowing, including international sovereign bonds first issued in 2007. Exports fell as a share of GDP while foreign debt grew.

Tax cuts in late 2019, the Easter Sunday attacks' blow to tourism, COVID-19, a sudden ban on chemical fertiliser in 2021 and falling foreign reserves led to shortages of fuel, cooking gas and medicines. In April 2022 the government suspended payments on most external debt, the country's first sovereign default.

The Central Bank raised interest rates sharply, the rupee was allowed to fall, taxes were raised, and an IMF programme was agreed in 2023. Inflation fell back to low levels, the economy returned to growth in 2024, and agreements with creditors restructured most of the external debt.

en.title: What money is
objectives: Explain the three functions of money
Trace how money evolved from commodities to digital balances
Explain why trust, not paper, gives money its value

learn.body: Without money, people must barter: a fisherman who wants rice must find a rice farmer who wants fish. This double coincidence of wants is rare, so trade stays small. Money solves the problem by being something everyone accepts, which lets people specialise and trade with strangers.

Money is a medium of exchange (used to pay), a unit of account (used to price and compare) and a store of value (used to carry purchasing power into the future). Money that fails at one of these, for example because prices rise very fast, starts to be replaced by something else, such as dollars or gold.

Early money had value in itself: cowrie shells across the Indian Ocean, gold and silver coins, even rice. Ancient Lankan kingdoms used coins of gold, silver and copper. Commodity money is trusted because the material is valuable, but its supply depends on mining or harvests, not on the needs of the economy.

learn.h: From convertible paper to fiat money
learn.body: Banknotes began as promises to pay gold or silver. Under the Bretton Woods system after 1944, currencies were tied to the US dollar, which was tied to gold. That link ended in 1971. Today's money is fiat money: it has value because the law makes it legal tender and people trust that others will accept it.

The rupee became Ceylon's currency in 1872, replacing earlier currencies. Since 1950 the Central Bank of Sri Lanka has issued it. Its value inside the country depends on inflation; its value outside depends on the exchange rate, which in turn depends on trust in the economy and its policies.

Notes and coins are only a small share of the money people use. Most is balances in bank accounts, moved by cards, transfers and QR payments. In India, UPI payments dwarf cash for many everyday purchases in cities, and central banks from China to India are testing digital versions of cash.

If people expect money to lose value fast, they spend it quickly or switch to other assets, which pushes prices up further. Zimbabwe in 2008 and Venezuela in the late 2010s saw hyperinflation and widespread use of US dollars. Protecting the value of money is the core job of a central bank.

en.title: Banks and how money is created
objectives: Read a simple bank balance sheet
Explain how bank lending creates deposits
Describe what limits money creation and why bank runs happen

learn.body: A bank takes deposits, makes loans and runs the payment system. It earns the gap between what it charges borrowers and pays depositors. Because only a small share of depositors withdraw on any day, a bank can lend most of the money it holds while keeping some in reserve.

A bank's assets are what it owns or is owed: loans, government securities, reserves at the central bank and cash. Its liabilities are what it owes: mainly customers' deposits and borrowing. The difference is equity, the owners' capital, which absorbs losses if loans go bad.

When a bank makes a loan, it credits the borrower's account with a new deposit. No one else's deposit falls. This is how most money in a modern economy is created. When loans are repaid, that money disappears. So the amount of money depends heavily on how much banks lend.

Banks keep reserves at the central bank to settle payments with each other. Many central banks set a minimum, the statutory reserve ratio. The Central Bank of Sri Lanka's ratio has been 2% of deposits since 2020. The textbook money multiplier links reserves to deposits, but in practice lending is limited more by demand, profitability, capital and regulation.

Narrow money (M1) is cash plus current account deposits. Broad money adds savings and fixed deposits: Sri Lanka publishes M2 and M2b. Watching the growth of broad money and private credit helps central banks judge whether demand is too strong or too weak.

Banks must hold capital, their own funds, as a share of their risk-weighted assets under rules based on the Basel framework. More capital means a bank can absorb losses without failing. Regulators also set liquidity rules so that banks can meet withdrawals.

If depositors fear a bank will fail, they may all try to withdraw at once. Even a healthy bank cannot repay everyone instantly, because its money is lent out. Deposit insurance, central bank lending in a crisis and strong supervision reduce the risk of runs. Silicon Valley Bank in the US collapsed in 2023 after a fast, online run.
